# Copper September 2010 

- Since flirting with cash lows of c.$6000/t ($2.72/lb) in early June, copper prices have responded strongly due to both constructive fundamentals and some supportive financials, and September’s six-month highs approaching $8000/t ($3.63/lb) do not appear to be the end of the bull run. 

- Following last year’s near 4% downturn in metal demand, we have noticed a continued pick-up in refined copper offtake, whether it has initially been due to the need to re-stock, or subsequently in end-user demand itself.  The 8.5% improvement anticipated this year already takes us beyond the former global record demand level of 17.955Mt set in 2008, and if it were not for some of the more systemic lingering issues (such as tighter credit availability), the copper market probably would have forgotten all about the “global economic crisis” already.  Looking at the bald numbers alone, then, one could say that in terms of copper demand, we have made a “recovery” – and somewhat sooner than everyone was expecting. 

- With LME Week rapidly approaching, concentrate buyers and sellers will be in the throes of finalising their ideas as to how the market may pan out in 2011.  And, despite the lack of interest in the spot market of late, our numbers still show that mine supplies will continue to underperform in relation to primary smelting capacity requirements over the next few years, leading to ongoing low overall primary smelter capacity utilisation rates.  For 2010, we estimate that the primary smelting industry will operate at just below 80% of its overall capacity. 

- There was a very marked shift in the spot market during September with many players caught by surprise at the sudden upswing in terms.  Miners are now being offered terms in the 50s & 5s by traders and rates in China have shot up to at least $50/t & 5c/lb from last month’s $20/t & 2c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper prices testing $8000/t mark once again** Since flirting with cash lows of c.$6000/t ($2.72/lb) in early June, copper prices have responded strongly due to both constructive fundamentals and some supportive financials, and September’s six-month highs

approaching $8000/t ($3.63/lb) do not appear to be the end of the bull run.  Ending August on $7355/t (cash, $3.34/lb), copper added a further $300/t in the first week of this month under favourable manufacturing sector data from the USA and China.  That early month high of $7660/t ($3.47/lb) on the 6th fell away sharply, though, the following day as rumours circulated of a copper stock sell-off from China’s State Reserve Bureau (SRB), and cash prices ended 1.8% down on the 7th at $7520/t ($3.41/lb).  That slide was swiftly reversed within 24 hours when the latest data release from the International Copper Study Group showed strong supply-demand fundamentals to May this year and underscored the message of market tightness that most analysts have been saying for the past few months.  Cash once again returned to the $7620/t mark ($3.46/lb).  Poor factory orders data out of Germany on the 8th, however, brought out the bears looking to test the $7500/t level.  Furthermore, although there was nothing to substantiate those SRB rumours, the dent into the red metal’s price push was then supported by a sustained strengthening of the dollar against the euro.  For the next four days copper prices lost half of their prior gains to end at $7525/t ($3.41/lb) on the 10th. 

**Shanghai stock reduction prompted mid-month push** From that low on the 10th, copper prices through to the end of the month rarely looked back.  Kicking off this most recent surge was the news on the 13th that stocks in Shanghai had fallen the prior week by a further 7.5% to 98kt, the lowest level since the end of January this year.  This news was supported by preliminary August trade data that showed strong refined copper net imports of 379kt, up by 11% on July’s 342kt.  But the importance of the statistic was not the rise per se, but that it took place during a month when any LME:SHFE arbitrage play was not feasible, and, consequently, the message to be drawn from this was that real Chinese metal demand was fundamentally strong.  Contributing also to the $100/t gain in cash prices on that day was news from Mexico that Grupo Mexico’s subsidiary Southern Peru Copper Corp had declared force majeure at its La Caridad integrated operations in Sonora.  As the mine-mill continues to operate, the only real impact on the market will be the added delay in getting the concentrates converted elsewhere. 

**Aurubis confident of copper demand going forward – macro data supportive** While profit-taking on the 14-15th of the third Wednesday of the month took the energy out of that price rise, some encouraging macro-economic news from the US regarding industrial production growth of 0.2% in August and a small increase in capacity utilisation brought sufficient renewed confidence to overwhelm the debate about declining European economies slipping into another round of financial malaise.  At the same time, management from one of Europe’s leading copper processors – Aurubis – expressed confidence that copp

**Chinese holidays not a factor as prices remain well supported** It was around this time, mid-month, that the metals complex as a whole was keeping an eye to the two sets of holidays that would keep Chinese market participants away from business during late September (Chinese Moon holidays, for three days) and into early October (National Day, for one week). Whilst traders did note some slowing of physical activity, copper prices remained firm to close out that week at $7756/t ($3.52/lb cash) on the 17th. Again, management-labour relations issues in Peru, plus a potential strike at Codelco’s Radomiro Tomic, came into view after markets closed on the 16th to provide that next-day price support. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - September 2010 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Dollar weakness against the euro matches copper’s price strength** Vying for first place in this month’s copper price movement analysis, alongside the usual supply-demand fundamentals has been the shifting relationship between the two principal Western currencies. Earlier, we mentioned how the stronger dollar had matched up with declining copper prices, and so the reverse came true for most of the second half of this month; fairly or otherwise, this currency interplay took the lion’s share of the responsibility according to many analysts for copper’s strengthening prices as we ended the month. As the dollar slipped toward 1.34 to the euro, so the likelihood of copper approaching $8000/t ($3.63/lb) increasingly came into view: closing cash prices on the 28th stood at $7948/t ($3.61/lb). This is not to say that the currency relationship is driving the copper price direction, just that for many market observers and perhaps makers, it is a contributing factor, and the argument then ensues as to whether the dollar will improve its standing going forward via domestic economic and industrial resurgence before the tightening measures of the European economies take hold into 2011, as they surely must do. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 Refined Imports 400

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - September 2010 Page 3 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Spot premia hold firm in USA, some strengthening in Europe** Equally, stocks have also fallen in the USA on Comex, from end-August’s 86.5kt (metric) to 77.5kt on September 28th, with the main depot changes being seen at El Paso (-4.2kt) and Salt Lake City (-2.3kt). Premia in the USA remained firm at c.6-6.3c/lb, while in Europe Standard cathode has edged up $5/t to $25/t, and Grade A material has, in some instances and locations, been commanding US$95/t instead of the more common $80-85/t range, and reflects the ongoing strength in copper demand. **Demand levels far better than expected…** Following last year’s near 4% downturn in metal demand, we have noticed a continued pick-up in refined copper off-take, whether it has initially been due to the need to re-stock, or subsequently in end-user demand itself. The 8.5% improvement anticipated this year already takes us beyond the former global record demand level of 17.955Mt set in 2008, and if it were not for some of the more systemic lingering issues (such as tighter credit availability), the copper market probably would have forgotten all about the “global economic crisis” already. Looking at the bald numbers alone, then, one could say that in terms of copper demand, we have made a “recovery” – and somewhat sooner than everyone was expecting. Anticipated growth for the next two years of between 5-6% should tap into the improving construction markets globally which, arguably, will be the last important sector to “recover”. **..and contrast with supply tightness** As we outlined last month, primary copper supply growth during the first half has been restricted due to low availability of concentrate feed, and smelters/refiners have had to turn to secondary materials to bridge the gap. We expect global refined copper production to increase by just 2.7% this year to ~18.8Mt. 2011’s refined production growth of 3.4%, and even the following year’s 7.5%, will be insufficient to outweigh our anticipated demand growth over the period, however, leaving us with a deficit of 420kt in 2011 and a balanced market for 2012. **Firmer market balance in H2 brings hike in price forecast** The traditionally slow third quarter has thus far exh

ibited stronger demand than usual, and consequently we have adjusted our consumption estimates since our last report by 30kt to reflect that strength. Equally, supply side issues have left Q3 refined production down by 12kt, leaving the surplus that we were showing last month of 69kt at just 33kt. With the second half in a balanced market, and turning to an annual deficit into 2011, we have increased our price forecasts for this year to $7335/t ($3.33/lb), and for 2011 to $8050/t ($3.65/lb), with the quarterly averages increasing to reflect the building deficits as we go through the year. Although 2012 should see new mine projects continuing to come through, we believe that the rate of ramp up will be lower than the project proponents would wish, and this will leave that year subject to a market closer to balance than we had previously expected. Consequently, we should see high prices of $7975/t ($3.62/lb) remaining as a feature of the market in that year. **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

Equally, upward revisions to demand data for 2009 in the USA offset minor losses elsewhere to leave last year’s demand down by a smaller -3.6% (vs. -3.8%) on 2008 at 17.3Mt. This year’s recovery is now looking to be healthier than our prior forecast of 18.675Mt and takes global demand up to 18.792Mt, with most regions sharing in the wide

spread improvement.  This is far beyond the pre-crisis 2008 demand level of just below 18Mt, and reflects the general disparity between apparent metals demand and the day-to-day sentiment of economic malaise. 

**Stronger 2010 recovery puts 2011 year-on-year growth lower** Having increased our forecast demand growth for 2010, the year-on-year percentage growth for next year is slightly lower at 5.8% vs. the 5.9% we were predicting in our August report.  However, in volume terms 2011 is 100kt higher at almost 19.9Mt.  While Chinese demand growth is leading the way, it is by no means the only geographic region of strength in the near term.  We expect European demand to increase by 5.3% this year and a further 1.4% in 2011, and North American demand to rise by 4.3% in 2010 and by 2% next year.  Over the near term, however, it is Chinese copper use and Asian demand in general which will sustain the metal going forward.  China’s continued investment and need to modernise should keep copper demand at a long-term rate of 6% p.a., while Asian and Latin American developing economies will also chip in with demand growth rates of between 4.5-5% p.a.  Thus global refined copper consumption will rise from 17.3Mt at the end of 2009 to 20.9Mt by 2012, and to 21.7Mt by 2013. 

### **Americas** 

**US focus on economic data belies metals demand strength** Of all the major economies, the focus on day-to-day economic data releases seems to drive national sentiment in the US more so than anywhere else, and this has created a division of opinions between those who see the economy picking up and those who do not.  As of this month, the USA is officially out of recession, but the run-up to the important November elections will continue to focus on the poor employment figures and the heavily flawed “debate” over personal taxation rates.  Meanwhile, for much of this year, metals demand has far outpaced most expectations, with manufacturing activity having been much stronger than expected. 

**Improvement in wire rod demand** Reflecting the improvement in manufacturing activity, US demand for copper wire rod, according to the American Bureau of Metals Statistics, increased during the second quarter for the first time since Q4 2007 – although we should bear in mind that Q2 2009 was the worst quarterly period in history.  H1 rod demand was up by 4.6% on the same period last year.  June domestic shipments were 18.4% higher than a year ago at 110.7kt, the highest since March.  Furthermore, rod inventories were down by 25% at the end of June vs. end-April’s 27.6kt at 20.4kt, and even though this could have been partly due to some summer shutdowns, it leaves the potential open for a sharp improvement in Q3 demand.  July’s rod data also show some positive indications, given that it is traditionally one of the slowest months.  Rod output at 113.7kt was up by 4.8% in June and by 10.1% for the seven months of this year vs. 2009.  Equally, domestic rod shipments were up by 10.6% to

July.  Apparent rod consumption of 105.6kt in July was up by 16.5% vs. July 2009, and even though we remain some way below the high levels seen in 2007 and 2008, the rising trends currently in place are encouraging as we enter the final quarter. 

**US tube makers benefit from trade investigation** US copper and copper alloy semis output of 409kt (metric) for January to May this year was up by 13% on the same period last year and, according to our sources, reflected the improved demand due to a combination of re-stocking and the possible introduction of an anti-dumping duty on copper tube imports from both Mexico and China.  Copper tube manufacturers reported to us that the rising interest in copper tube reflected the joint investigation by the Commerce Department and International Trade Commission (ITC) into whether imports of Mexican and Chinese copper tube were being sold below market value in the US.  US tube petitioners were Cerro Flow Products, Kobe Wieland Copper Products LLC, Mueller Copper Tube Products and Mueller Copper Tube Co which took the opinion that the 42kt of products imported from China in 2009 along with 22kt from Mexico were sold below cost.  In the middle of August the Commerce Department and the ITC introduced a preliminary dumping margin of 30.9% on all Mexican tube imports (with 29.52% on those from producer IUSA and 32.27% on those from Nacobre, specifically) and a margin of between 10.26% and 60.5% on all Chinese tube imports.  A final ruling from Commerce came on September 27th, and issued final calculated dumping rates of between 11.25% on products from the Golden Dragon Precise Copper Tube Group to 60.85% on those from the Zhejiang Hailiang Group, and between 24.89% on products from IUSA to 31.43% on products from Nacobre.  The ITC will make its final determination on November 8th, and if it agrees with these findings, Commerce will issue anti-dumping orders against the companies cited. 

**Brazilian copper demand remains healthy** Brazil’s copper sector, as represented by Sindicel, has reported a generally favourable first half this year, with almost half of the 51 copper-using members which cover 90% of national demand reporting growth of 10% or more during Q2 over the first quarter of this year.  Exchange rate stability, plus an improvement in credit availability, have contributed to the general improvement in business sentiment and sales.  Output of wire rod at the country’s largest facility at Caraiba, owned by Paranapanema, exceeded 55kt during the first half,

representing a significant improvement on full-year 2009’s 89kt.  The government’s plans to upgrade the country’s power network will also provide support to future refined copper demand.  Thus we forecast that Brazilian refined copper demand will increase by 4% this year, to 350kt, and by a slightly stronger 5.1% in 2011 to just below 368kt. 

**Mexico’s ro

d production may stall** Wire rod production at Grupo Mexico’s La Caridad plant, which produced 60.1kt last year, has been put on a force majeure notice, along with the rest of the facility, owing to a labour dispute (see Page 15). We were expecting rod output of c.74kt this year from La Caridad, but now this figure will most likely need revising. The plant has a rated 150kt/a capacity, and is second largest after Condumex’s Conticon at Celaya (180kt/a), in Guanajuato. Condumex would try to increase its presence in the market if La Caridad indeed stays off line for some time. But it is unlikely to benefit significantly from the export market. Unlike Brazil, Mexico’s economy is heavily reliant on its northern neighbour. When the US slid into recession, Mexico’s manufacturing sector was dragged down. However, with the US manufacturing sector expanding, Mexican manufacturing, particularly the automotive sector, has been boosted. This was reflected in car production increasing by 49% year on year during the first five months of the year. While this rate of recovery is not expected to be maintained throughout the remainder of the year, orders for copper wiring and copper semi products from the auto sector will help support copper demand growth this year. Thus we forecast that Mexican refined copper consumption will increase by 4.7% this year, to 290kt, and by 5.2% in 2011 to 305kt. #### **US brass mill shipments – (kt)** 30 95

### **China** **The growth of China's industrial value-added output accelerated to 13.9% y-o- in August from July's 13.4%** The growth rate for the first eight months was 16.6%, down 0.4% from the January to July period. The strength in heavy industrial production and fixed investment may in part be due to a re-stocking after the de-stocking in early summer and after the government emphasised the importance of maintaining growth at the end of July. However, some local governments became increasingly worried about achieving their energy efficiency targets and started to cut power to energy-intensive sectors at the end of August. If investment, and hence demand, for heavy industrial products, continues to hold up stronger than expected for the rest of the year, then achieving the energy efficiency target will have to rely more on supply restraint – power cuts and capacity closures. **Domestic demand was stronger than expected** China's retail sales of consumer goods in August increased by 18.4% year-on-year; urban consumption was up 18.8% and rural consumption increased by 15.9%. Housing sales volume started to recover in August, and this trend might continue to the end of this year. **Mixed real estate measures** Floor space for new-build housing inc

reased by 66.1% year-on-year in the first eight months, reflecting more new housing projects under construction.  However, figures for floor space of completed housing increased by less than 11% to July, and it actually fell by 2.1% in August, reflecting that some investors have postponed completing the projects due to current weak demand, and this will have a knock-on effect for building wire and associated construction products.

**August exports continued to weaken** While year-ago growth was a strong 34.4%, the August change fell a large 2.7%, and it was the third consecutive decline.  Imports increased by 2.5% m/m, after falling for two consecutive months. The year-ago change was also a higher 35.2%.  The stronger result is consistent with growing signs of stabilisation in the heavy industrial sector, while also suggesting that exports are softening, but not collapsing.  Compared with the high base of Q4 2009, China’s economic growth will continue to slow.  Q4 GDP growth should be in the region of 8.0-8.5% year-on-year due to the impact of the property tightening, energy saving measures, and the expected soft exports. 

**White goods sales continue to increase in August…** Data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology report continued high sales of home appliances through August.  Output of refrigerators, air conditioners and washing machines increased by 26.3%, 37.2% and 35.5%, respectively, during the first eight months of the year vs. the same period in 2009. 

**..but lower ACR tube output noted last month** Despite the above encouraging set of statistics, however, we believe that ACR tube production specifically continued to slow down in August due to the falling demand for air conditioning and lower exports.  Imposing preliminary dumping rates on imported refined copper tube from China in the USA (see story above) began to take their toll on Chinese exports of ACR tube since May.  Total Chinese inner-grooved copper tube exports to August  were down by 17.5% to 33.672kt, and we expect ACR tube exports will continue to fall in the coming months because of the disruption to suppliers.  Usually, air conditioner makers need three months to test new ACR tube in their production lines, and after this time we would expect that US-based air conditioner makers will change their Chinese ACR tube suppliers.  With the US market now largely out of reach, Chinese ACR tube exporters will continue their focus on other Asian and Mid-East consumers, such as South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, India and Saudi Arabia. 

**High-end connector strip falls away in September** The market for high-end connector strip continued to be soft in early September, and we doubt that we will see any pick-up in order books before mid-October, given the one week holiday in the early October. Normally September should be the high season for connector production. The

falling demand might reflect the high inventory of electronic industry products and soft exports order of some home electrical appliances. The demand for lead frame strip remains strong, but some frame strip manufacturers forecast that an inventory correction can be expected in October, and so we should expect to see disappointing order books ahead. **Wire rod markets flat in early September** There are no signs that wire rod production in September has improved over August, and this is contrary to the expectations of most wire rod makers. De-stocking by auto makers and the slowdown in the export markets of some electrical home appliances represent some of the reasons at least for this aberration. Some major copper fabricators in Zhejiang province mentioned that electricity supply has been better in September than in August due to the falling electricity demand from air conditioning use. But the constraints on power use in Zhejiang province are expected to endure until the end of this year. **Power industry investment up marginally** According to the latest data issued by China Electricity Council, the investment in power industry in the first eight months reached 365.9Bn RMB ($54.4Bn), increasing by 1.7% year-onyear. Investments in power generation increased by 15.5% year-on-year, reaching 196.6Bn RMB ($29.2Bn) and it accounted for 53.7% of total power industry investment. Investment in the power grid fell by 11.1% year-on-year, and this explains the ongoing weakness in the demand for power cable. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - September 2010 Page 7 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **Double-digit growth in Chinese copper demand expected this year and next** This year, despite all the debate and concern regarding the enforced slowdown in the Chinese economy, we remain confident that copper demand will increase by 13% year-on-year to 7.3Mt. In 2011 we forecast that the dissipation of the impact of the government’s stimulus packages and last year’s surge in lending will be more than offset by strong demand for Chinese exports which will lift Chinese copper consumption by a further 10% to ~8.1Mt. Equally, although the country’s primary copper-refining sector has drawn down on large supplies of scrap, we believe that there has not been a comparable appetite for scrap from the semis sector. By our calculations, scrap use in semis will increase by between 4.0-4.5% this year on 2009, while semis output should rise by c.12-15% year on year; meanwhile, preliminary semis output data for August show a near 18% increase, year-on-year, and net import growth of 26.5% at 271kt. **Ongoing investments in new plant** We conti

nue to note new copper-consuming semis plants are being built and commissioned in China. In August and into this month, Huana International (Tongling) Electronic Material Co announced that its 10kt/a electronic foil plant at Tongling City, Anhui, was commissioned on August 9th. This doubles Huana’s foilmaking capacity. Mingwang Copper Semis has decided to add a 5kt/a production line to its existing 10kt/a Cu-Al semis plant at Lanzhou City, Gansu at a cost of 36M Yuan, focusing on copper and brass bars. And Jinyu Copper Co is investing 200M Yuan in a new, four-line copper tube plant at Xichuan, Henan, which will start in August 2011. ### **Europe** **European copper demand increased to 3.61Mt** We have increased our forecast for European copper demand this year from 3.567Mt to 3.61Mt since our August report, given the stronger first half of the year than previously anticipated. Equally, we had been under the impression that early August indicators showed lower performances than in July, but now we believe that this was more a reflection of summer shut-downs rather than the start of the more widespread downturn in business levels. Wire rod producers in Western Europe are reportedly working their facilities “flat out”, but end-user demand is not all from this region but from the former East Bloc nations such as Poland and Romania. We reported last month our unconfirmed belief that Romania’s sole rod producer – Cuprom – had closed, and now the company has made that official by acknowledging that it stopped making rod at its Zalau facility in September 2009. Since then, it has been importing all of its c.30-40kt annualised of rod in order to keep its wire-making lines busy, and this squares with reports that we have heard of strong rod demand from the Former East Europe region. **KME looking to positive second half** KME, which claims to be the world’s largest semis fabricator, selling 437kt of copper and alloy semis in 2009 from manufacturing plants in Germany, Italy, France, UK, Spain and China, reported a 21% (+46kt, to 264kt) increase in its output of copper and copper alloy products in H1 from a year earlier. Robust orders from the auto and electronics sectors and domestic appliance manufacturing helped to offset weak demand from the construction sector, which accounts for 40% of KME’s sales by application. Until recently, spot rates were far too low for most buyers which limited the purchasing pool to just China and India, leaving smelters elsewhere to adjust their primary operating rates to match what they could buy under their long-term contracts. However, over the past few months both of the major Indian buyers were noticeably absent from the market while more recently it has been the turn of the Chinese smelters to refrain from making (almost any) spot purchases. Some market observers believe that there has been a concerted effort on the part of the Chinese to stay away from the market in order to force terms higher. Others point to various events such a lack of arbitrage opportunities, maintenance downtime and production problems at various Chinese smelters as to the root cause of this. Whatever the truth may be, exceedingly thin trading conditions have seen spot buying and selling rates rise very significantly over the past few weeks. The only tender of any note apparently secured terms in the mid 40s & 4s, although miners are now being offered terms in the 50s & 5s by traders and rates in China have shot up to at least $50/t & 5c/lb from last month’s $20/t & 2c/lb. Note that these current terms are indicative only given that it has become incredibly difficult to sell any material into this market at present. Elsewhere in India, terms have also increased substantially, again moving to in excess of $50/t & 5c/lb by month end, with the enforced closure of Sterlite’s 400kt/a Tuticorin smelter expected to fuel a further uplift in spot rates in the short term. #### **Concentrate market TC/RCs** ||**Te**|**Japanese**

C **hina’s appetite for imported copper concentrates continues to wane** China’s appetite for foreign copper concentrates continued to wane with imports in August (474.5kdmt) declining year on year (-10.3%) for the fourth consecutive month.  Cumulative receipts during the first eight months of 2010 were 4.28Mdmt which remain a little ahead (+3.8%) of last year’s comparable level but only on account of the strong start to 2010.  As mentioned, som

e market observers believe that there is a concerted effort within China to avoid buying spot concentrates in order to force terms up, particularly just ahead of the start of the long-term Mating Season.  However, there are a number of other factors that could be contributing to this general reluctance to buy spot cargos.  Many Chinese buyers speculate on the market (i.e. buying in a rising market and/or arbitraging SHFE prices against the LME etc.) in order to improve the profitability of their concentrate purchases.  However, these speculative opportunities have not been that evident of late which has no doubt dampened buying enthusiasm.  Also, blister and particularly scrap have been relatively more abundant this year and, with general liquidity amongst China’s smelters and refiners considerably better than in the country’s consuming sector, this has enabled the former to purchase more good quality scrap than might otherwise have been the case.  We also hear that a number of smelters have experienced operational difficulties, including Baiyin, Huludao, Jinlong, Yantai and Zhongtiaoshan (in addition to the extended maintenance shutdown at Yunnan’s Kunming smelter) which has caused some to resell concentrates to other buyers within the domestic market.  We currently expect that Chinese imports of copper concentrates will be flat on last year; i.e. at around 6.1Mdmt. 

**China’s reluctance to buy spot concentrates unlikely to be sustainable** Whatever the reason for the decline in Chinese imports in recent months, most commentators agree that the current situation is unsustainable.  There is, for example, a finite level of scrap that can be consumed in conventional primary smelters without upsetting, in particular converter heat balances.  There is general agreement that the next Chinese concentrate buying spree will be substantial in order to replace significantly depleted inventories.  However, this may not start in earnest until later this year or perhaps at the very latest around Chinese New Year.  As we have discussed in previous reports there is a considerable amount of additional Chinese smelting capacity in the pipeline and new potential additions continue to be added to this growing list of projects.  The latest announcements have come from Hunan Shuikoushan Nonferrous Metals Group Co., Ltd (the creator of the SKS furnace) and Western Mining Holdings Co., Ltd.  Both companies aim to establish 100kt/a smelter/refinery projects with a view to increasing these to an eventual 200kt/a.  Neither of these projects has received EIA approval as yet and so the likelihood of their development remains uncertain.  Elsewhere, Jiangxi Copper has plans for a major expansion of a relocated Yantai smelter/refinery if plans to acquire the company come to fruition.  Yantai had aimed to build a new 100kt/a complex while Jiangxi’s concept is for a 300kt/a smelter/refinery project.

With the inclusion of the Tintaya-Antapaccay projects the company’s Southern Peru division should be capable of producing in excess of 500kt/a Cu by the end of 2014. 

**La Caridad smelter/refinery affected by union unrest** As mentioned and according to Southern Copper, since September 2nd supporters of the mining union leader Napoleon Gomez have been using violence and intimidation to prevent workers at the 250kt/a La Caridad smelter and refinery from entering the complex.  The miner’s union led by Gomez lost the collective contract at La Caridad in 2007 to a more moderate union but has been trying to re-establish its presence ever since.  As a consequence of this action the company has declared force majeure on shipments from the complex.  Last year La Caridad produced 1171.kt of refined copper and 60.1kt of wire rod.  During H1 2010 the equivalent figures were 65kt and 36kt respectively.  Output at the La Caridad smelter/refinery complex has been constrained over the past three years by the closure of the Cananea mine which is expected to be reactivated during H1 2011.  However, repairs and reconstruction activity at Cananea continues to be hampered by clashes breaking out between dismissed Cananea union members and company contract workers. 

**Madras Court orders Sterlite’s Tuticorin smelter to shut down on environmental grounds** On September 29th Sterlite Industries was forced to close its 400kt/a smelter in Tuticorin after being issued with an order to do so by the Madras High Court.  The order relates to a case that was filed in 1996 in relation to environmental issues.  The order apparently stated that the smelter’s activities would result in a rise in pollution levels and affect workers at the Tuticorin plant.  Under Indian law Sterlite could appeal the High Court decision in the Supreme Court by filing a stay against the Order.  We would be surprised if the closure were to be long-lasting on the basis of the ability of the Tuticorin smelter to comply with environmental regulations given that the plant employs very modern technology in terms of its furnace (IsaSmelt) and gas capturing and handling facilities.  However, for now the company is expected to lose 1kt/d of refined copper while the smelter remains closed. 

**KGHM sources extra copper-bearing materials - lifts 2010 production estimate** Poland’s KGHM recently raised its 2010 production estimate from its three metallurgical operations from 512kt of refined copper to 541kt.  The increase has been brought about primarily on account of an increase in purchased copper-bearing materials and in particular scrap. As mentioned, high copper prices have resulted in a surge of scrap throughout Europe enabling KGHM to acquire more than had been expected.
